🚨Federal Judge Declines to Block Trump’s Mail-In Ballot Verification Order Ahead of 2026 Midterms Washington, D.C., U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols on May 28 declined to immediately halt President Donald Trump’s executive order directing federal agencies to create verified lists of U.S. citizens for mail-in voting, ruling that a challenge by Democratic groups was premature. Judge Nichols said that no concrete harm had yet occurred because the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Social Security Administration (SSA) have not finalized the citizenship lists or begun sharing these with states. Executive order 14399 titled, "Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections," signed March 31, also directs USPS to deliver mail-in and absentee ballots only to voters on those approved lists and requires states to retain certain election records for five years. The executive order aims to strengthen election integrity by using federal databases to confirm citizenship and prevent ballots from reaching non-citizens or ineligible voters ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration says. It does not ban mail voting nor impose a new national voter ID requirement but relies on existing federal records for verification in federal elections. Democratic plaintiffs, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, along with voting rights groups such as the NAACP and LULAC, sued the Trump administration arguing the unconstitutionally of the EO stating that it intrudes on states’ authority to run elections under the Constitution’s Elections Clause. They also warned that incomplete federal databases could wrongly exclude eligible citizens — especially seniors, low-income voters and naturalized citizens — potentially disenfranchising millions and sowing chaos before tight congressional races. Judge Nichols on Thursday did not rule on the order’s legality and left open the possibility for the plaintiffs to refile once agencies take concrete steps causing actual harm. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown is co-leading a coalition of 23 attorneys general and one governor in a separate lawsuit filed in early April challenging this same March 31 executive order. Currently, states are preparing voter rolls. Ballot delivery systems are under the threat of federal funding cuts or enforcement actions for noncompliance. The executive order’s citizenship-list requirement and USPS restrictions on ballot delivery would require changes to Washington state’s vote-by-mail system, including how ballots are tracked and delivered. AG Brown's suit argues the president lacks authority to unilaterally overhaul state election procedures and that the changes would force rapid, costly alterations to voter rolls, registration and mail-ballot processes just months before primaries and the general election. Brown's coalition suit builds on an earlier successful challenge by Washington and Oregon against a related 2025 Trump executive order. In that April 2025 case, the states blocked provisions requiring documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration and stricter ballot receipt deadlines. Washington counts ballots postmarked by Election Day even if they arrive later; more than 250,000 such ballots were accepted in the 2024 general election.

🚨👂This is Stopable — primarily through ongoing federal court challenges, with a realistic chance of being blocked or significantly delayed before the 2026 midterms. Current Status (as of June 1, 2026) • The USPS proposed rule (issued May 29/30, 2026) is in the public comment period and not final. A final rule could come later, but implementation timelines are tight for November midterms. • Multiple lawsuits (from Democratic states, voting rights groups like League of Women Voters, Brennan Center, ACLU, etc.) are active in D.C. and Massachusetts federal courts. They argue the EO and rule unconstitutionally usurp state election authority (Elections Clause), violate federalism/Tenth Amendment, overstep presidential power over USPS, and burden voting rights. Key Legal Developments • On May 28/29, 2026, U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols (Trump appointee) declined a preliminary injunction, ruling challenges were “premature” because no final agency actions (like the USPS rule) had occurred yet and plaintiffs hadn’t shown concrete harm. He explicitly left the door open: plaintiffs can refile once implementation steps happen. • The new USPS proposed rule strengthens plaintiffs’ standing for renewed injunction requests. Hearings (e.g., in Boston on June 2) and updated motions are expected soon. Past precedent: Similar provisions in Trump’s 2025 EO were blocked by multiple federal courts on separation-of-powers and federalism grounds. Appeals are ongoing, but lower courts have been skeptical of broad executive rewriting of election rules. Other Ways It Could Be Stopped or Limited • Congress: Legislation (e.g., Sen. Padilla’s proposed bill) could nullify the EO or restrict USPS implementation, but this faces partisan hurdles and filibuster issues. • States: Non-cooperation (refusing data sharing or using workarounds) could create practical obstacles, though it risks legal/funding fights. • USPS itself: As an independent agency, full resistance or slow-walking is possible, but political appointees are pushing forward. • Practical delays: Rulemaking, data systems, and logistics make full rollout before 2026 unlikely even without courts, per some analysts. Bottom line: Courts are the main brake. With the rule now public, expect accelerated litigation. Many legal experts and opponents believe it will ultimately be enjoined (at least key parts) due to constitutional limits on presidential power over state-run elections. Supporters argue it’s lawful use of federal mail authority and will survive. The outcome depends on appeals, potential Supreme Court involvement, and timing — but yes, it’s very much “stoppable” in its current form.
